title: How to Make Stress Work for You
author: Christian Poensgen
summary: A guest post on Nir Eyal's newsletter by an executive coach whose doctoral work compared stress and performance, arguing that the body emits one arousal signal and the person supplies its meaning. Poensgen opens with the finding that his instruments could not distinguish stress from excitement, so he had to ask participants which one they were feeling. He then assembles the evidence that the interpretation is consequential: a large longitudinal study in which high stress raised mortality risk only among those who believed stress was harmful, and McGonigal's estimate that the belief itself accounts for twenty thousand American deaths a year. The heart of the piece is David Yeager's synergistic mindset, which pairs the belief that the stress response is a resource with the belief that stressful events are chances to grow, and which Yeager's trials found only worked when both were addressed together. Poensgen explains why each half fails alone, then gives three practices: a self-authored letter reframing the response, a second letter reframing the event in Dweck's growth terms, and a set of deliberately daunting stress goals so the arousal has somewhere to go. He closes by reading his own failed measurement as the real result rather than an equipment limitation.
points: The founding observation is methodological: heart rate and skin conductance could not tell a thrilled participant from a stressed one, so questionnaires had to do what sensors could not.
The mortality data cut both ways, with high-stress people who rejected the harm belief showing lower risk than those reporting the least stress of anyone.
Yeager's trials matter because they show the two beliefs are not additive but interdependent, each one covering for the other's failure mode.
A stress-is-enhancing mindset is described as pulling cortisol responders toward a healthier middle and clearing the response faster, which is how acute stress avoids becoming chronic.
Stress goals are presented as the anchor for both beliefs, on the reasoning that nothing meaningful is easy and nothing easy is particularly meaningful.
quotes: From a physiological perspective, stress looks almost identical to excitement. The same rise in heart rate. The same increase in skin conductance. I could not separate the two with the tracking devices we used.
Your body produces one signal. You add meaning afterward, based on what you already believe about stress.

The people under high stress who didn’t hold that belief had the lowest mortality risk in the sample, even lower than those who reported the least stress of anyone. Stress doesn’t kill you. Stress plus the belief that it’s harming you does.

Telling someone to see the challenge as an opportunity does nothing while their body is filing a contradictory report. And a racing heart won’t read as helpful to anyone who sees the challenge as a threat to their standing. Each belief has to cover for the other.
A stress-is-enhancing mindset pulls both extremes toward a healthier middle: the big responders spike less, the flat responders rise a little more, and both return to baseline faster.
People who believe stress is harmful lean on avoidant coping: distraction, emotional withdrawal, numbing. They work on escaping the feeling instead of treating it as a signal to act.
They’re designed to stretch your capacity, not for the sake of hardship but because nothing meaningful in life is easy, and nothing easy is particularly meaningful.
More than a decade later, I think that was the finding, not a limitation of the equipment. The signal is the same. What differs is the meaning you assign to it.
